test_title: RRB Group D Official Paper (Held On: 27 Dec, 2025 Shift 2)
subject: general
question: Which statement best describes an olfactory indicator?

options.text: A substance that changes smell in acids and bases
A liquid that changes colour in all solutions
A gas that reacts only with strong acids
A solid that dissolves in both acids and bases

solution:
The correct answer is __**A substance that changes smell in acids and bases**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Olfactory indicators** are substances whose **odor or smell changes** depending on whether they are mixed with an **acidic or a basic solution**.
 
• The term **"olfactory"** pertains to the **sense of smell**, and these indicators are primarily used in **chemistry laboratories** to test the nature of a particular substance when color-based indicators cannot be used.
 
• In an **acidic medium**, the characteristic smell of these indicators typically **remains the same** or does not disappear.
 
• In a **basic medium**, the characteristic smell of these indicators is usually **destroyed or cannot be detected**. ***Hence, statement 1 is correct.***
 
• A liquid that changes **color** in solutions refers to **visual indicators** like **Litmus, Phenolphthalein, or Methyl Orange**, but not specifically to olfactory ones. ***Hence, statement 2 is incorrect.***
 
• A gas that reacts only with **strong acids** or a solid that **dissolves** in both media does not define the functional property of an indicator meant for **pH detection** through smell. ***Hence, statements 3 and 4 are incorrect.***

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Common Examples of Olfactory Indicators:**
 
 
• **Onion:** When a cloth strip treated with **onion juice** is kept in a **base** like **Sodium Hydroxide (NaOH)**, the pungent smell of the onion **disappears**. However, in an **acid** like **Hydrochloric Acid (HCl)**, the smell persists.
 
• **Vanilla Essence:** The pleasant smell of **vanilla** vanishes when it is added to a **basic solution**. It retains its smell in **acidic solutions**.
 
• **Clove Oil:** The characteristic smell of **clove oil** also disappears in the presence of a **base** and remains detectable in the presence of an **acid**.
 
 
 
• **Synthetic Indicators:** Unlike olfactory indicators, synthetic indicators like **Phenolphthalein** are colorless in **acidic** solutions and turn **pink** in **basic** solutions. **Methyl Orange** turns **red** in acids and **yellow** in bases.
 
• **Natural Indicators:** Other natural indicators include **Turmeric** (which stays **yellow** in acid and turns **reddish-brown** in base) and **Red Cabbage juice**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Utility for Visually Impaired:** Olfactory indicators are highly significant for **visually impaired students** in science education. Since they cannot observe **color changes** in traditional indicators like **litmus paper**, they rely on the **change in odor** to identify the chemical nature of substances.
 
• **Chemical Reaction:** The change in smell occurs because the **acid or base** reacts with the **organic compounds** responsible for the scent in the indicator, effectively neutralizing or altering the molecules that the **olfactory receptors** detect.
 
• **pH Scale Context:** Indicators are used to determine if a substance has a **pH less than 7 (Acidic)** or a **pH greater than 7 (Basic)**. Olfactory indicators provide a **qualitative** rather than quantitative measure of this property.
</ul
